sections.content: As an employee, regularly solicit feedback from your boss first. Then offer praise as well as criticism; Scott notes that praise can encourage the boss to do more of what you appreciate. When raising criticism, begin from a neutral place rather than leading with the harshest version. Be ready to gauge its impact, and approach it humbly as a dialogue, making clear that you intend to help rather than claiming unquestionable authority.

sections.heading: How to respond to the boss’s reaction
sections.content: Pay attention to the boss’s emotional signals. If they seem to brush off the feedback, continue becoming more direct; Scott’s example moved from asking whether the boss noticed saying “um” to offering a blunt explanation of the impact. If the boss looks sad or mad, move toward more care personally. If they get angry, don’t yell back or retreat: get curious about why they are upset, acknowledge that you may not have said it in the right way, and affirm that the issue is important and needs to be resolved. Scott also endorses gauging reactions in person or by phone when possible, since communication is emotional as well as intellectual.

answer.summary: Solicit feedback regularly first, then give praise and criticism. When raising criticism with your boss, start neutrally and watch how it lands: become more direct if they brush it off, and show more care if they seem sad or angry. Stay curious and keep the issue in view rather than escalating or retreating.

sections.heading: How to approach the feedback
sections.content: Scott recommends an order of operations: regularly solicit feedback from your boss first, then offer both praise and criticism. When it is time to raise a concern, begin in a neutral way rather than leading with the harshest formulation. Be ready to gauge the response; having the conversation in person or by phone can help you read the other person’s emotional signals. (Scott agrees with the value of gauging the reaction, while the suggestion to use in-person or phone conversations is voiced by the interviewer.)

sections.heading: How to respond to the boss’s reaction
sections.content: If your boss seems to brush off the feedback, keep moving toward greater directness. Scott’s example starts with asking whether the boss noticed saying “um” frequently, then offering a speech-coach introduction; after both are dismissed, the feedback becomes more explicit. If your boss looks sad or mad, treat that as a cue to show more care. Take a beat to notice the emotion, avoid either yelling back or abandoning the point, and get curious rather than furious. Scott suggests a response along the lines of acknowledging you may not have said it the right way while making clear that the issue matters and needs to be resolved.
